functions.name: Communicator::customize_event_handler
functions.description: Install a custom event handler used for scheduling and waiting for events.
requirements: handler must implement schedule() and wait().
When to call (before/after init) and ownership/lifetime expectations are not documented.

functions.name: Communicator::~Communicator
functions.description: Virtual destructor for Communicator.
requirements: Call Communicator::deinit before destruction to ensure clean shutdown (best practice; not enforced by header).

functions.name: SleepRequest::SleepRequest
functions.description: Constructs a SleepRequest bound to a given CommScheduler. The instance will use the provided scheduler to schedule/unschedule its sleep operation when dispatched or canceled. Typical usage is to create an instance with a valid scheduler and then let the task framework invoke dispatch().
requirements: scheduler must be a valid, non-null pointer to a CommScheduler instance.
scheduler must remain valid for at least as long as the SleepRequest may call scheduler->sleep(this) or scheduler->unsleep(this) (i.e., for the lifetime of the SleepRequest or until its completion).

functions.name: SleepRequest::dispatch
functions.description: Submits this SleepRequest to its CommScheduler by calling scheduler->sleep(this). If the scheduler returns an error (value < 0), the request transitions to an error state via handle(SS_STATE_ERROR, errno) and completes the subtask. Intended to be invoked by the task framework as part of the SubTask lifecycle.
requirements: The SleepRequest object must have been constructed with a valid CommScheduler pointer.
May trigger asynchronous behavior via the scheduler; any result or error is communicated through handle(state, error) rather than a return value.
If scheduler->sleep(this) fails, errno is used to report the error; callers should not expect dispatch() to throw or return an error code.

functions.name: ExecRequest::ExecRequest
functions.description: Constructor that initializes an ExecRequest with a target execution queue and an executor. Typically used to bind the request to an Executor that will process it and an optional ExecQueue that selects where/how it is queued. No validation is performed; pointers are stored for later use by dispatch(). Details of ExecQueue/Executor behavior are defined elsewhere (unknown).
requirements: executor must be a valid, non-null pointer to an Executor instance; otherwise later calls (e.g., dispatch) will dereference a null pointer and crash
queue may be null or non-null; no checks are performed here (actual requirements depend on Executor::request and are unknown)
the ExecRequest object must be fully constructed before use in any SubTask/ExecSession workflow (implied by class inheritance)

functions.name: ExecRequest::get_request_queue
functions.description: Returns the currently associated ExecQueue pointer for this request. Useful to inspect or pass along the queue on which the request will be scheduled. May return null if no queue was set or was set to null.
requirements: call on a valid ExecRequest instance; method is const and does not modify state
returned pointer may be null; callers must handle a null queue safely

functions.name: ExecRequest::set_request_queue
functions.description: Sets or updates the ExecQueue associated with this request. The pointer is stored as-is and will be used during dispatch(). No ownership transfer or validity checks are performed.
requirements: queue may be null or non-null; no validation is performed
must be called before dispatch() if the desired queue differs from the one provided at construction

functions.name: ExecRequest::dispatch
functions.description: Attempts to submit this request to the associated Executor via executor->request(this, this->queue). On failure (executor->request returns a negative value), the request’s handle(state,error) is invoked with ES_STATE_ERROR and errno, and the subtask completes via subtask_done(). Intended entry point to schedule the request for execution within the Executor framework.
requirements: executor must be a valid, non-null pointer; otherwise this will dereference a null pointer and crash
may rely on queue being acceptable to Executor::request; if a specific queue is required, it must be set beforehand via constructor or set_request_queue() (exact constraints are unknown)
caller should be prepared that dispatch() may synchronously transition the task to an error state via handle(ES_STATE_ERROR, errno) if submission fails; errno is used as provided by the failing call
should be called within the expected lifecycle of SubTask/ExecSession objects as defined by the surrounding framework (details unknown)

functions.name: IORequest::IORequest
functions.description: Constructor that associates this IORequest with an IOService. The service will later be used to submit the request via IOService::request(this). Typical usage: create an IORequest with a valid IOService*, then call dispatch() to start the request. Details of IOService and the lifecycle are defined elsewhere.
requirements: service must be a valid, non-null pointer to an IOService instance
service is expected to be able to accept this object via IOService::request(IOSession*) (inferred from dispatch())
The IOService instance should remain valid for at least the duration of dispatch() and any asynchronous processing triggered by it (lifetime expectations inferred; exact duration unknown)

functions.name: IORequest::dispatch
functions.description: Submits this IORequest to its IOService. It calls service->request(this) and, if the return value is negative, it treats the operation as failed and calls handle(IOS_STATE_ERROR, errno). Intended entry point to start processing the IO request within the framework.
requirements: Must be called only after constructing IORequest with a valid, non-null service pointer
service->request(this) must be safe to call on the current thread/context as required by IOService (unknown specifics)
Caller should not assume synchronous completion; completion is signaled via handle/subtask_done() (as per framework pattern)
On failure, errno is used; caller should ensure errno is meaningful in the environment when request() returns < 0

functions.name: IORequest::handle
functions.description: Completion/error handler for the IORequest. Stores the provided state and error into the object and marks the subtask as done by invoking subtask_done(). In this class, handle sets terminal state and notifies completion; subclasses or framework code may call/override it to report progress or errors.
requirements: state should be a valid IOSession/IO state code (e.g., IOS_STATE_ERROR) recognized by the surrounding framework (exact valid values unknown)
error should be an error code compatible with the framework’s expectations (e.g., errno value when state indicates error)
Calling handle triggers subtask_done(); callers must ensure it is appropriate to mark the subtask as complete at this time
Intended to be called by the framework or subclass logic; external callers should not invoke protected methods directly

functions.name: ExecQueue::init
functions.description: Initializes an ExecQueue instance, preparing its internal list and mutex for use as a queue of execution sessions. Use before submitting or manipulating sessions associated with this queue.
requirements: Must be called before using this ExecQueue with Executor::request or other queue operations.
Should not be called more than once without a matching deinit() in between (idempotency unknown).
Thread-safety of concurrent init() calls on the same instance is unknown; avoid concurrent initialization.
Return value semantics (e.g., 0 for success) are unknown; callers must check and handle the returned int appropriately.

functions.name: ExecQueue::deinit
functions.description: Tears down an ExecQueue instance, releasing resources such as its mutex and clearing internal state. Call when the queue is no longer needed.
requirements: Should only be called on a queue that has been successfully initialized via init().
Must not be called while other threads are accessing the queue; ensure no in-flight operations reference this queue when deinitializing.
After deinit(), the queue instance must not be used again unless re-initialized with init().

functions.name: ExecQueue::~ExecQueue
functions.description: Destructor for ExecQueue. In this header it is defined as an empty inline virtual destructor. It does not perform deinitialization; use deinit() to release resources.
requirements: Do not rely on the destructor to free or release resources managed by init(); call deinit() explicitly before destruction.
Object must not be destroyed while other threads may access it.

functions.name: ExecSession::get_queue
functions.description: Returns the ExecQueue associated with this session. Useful inside derived session logic to inspect or interact with its queue. The association is managed internally (e.g., by the executor when a session is requested).
requirements: May return nullptr if the session has not been associated with a queue yet; callers must handle a null return.
The returned pointer must not be used after the queue has been deinitialized or destroyed.
Does not modify object state; callable on const ExecSession.

functions.name: ExecSession::~ExecSession
functions.description: Destructor for ExecSession. Defined as an empty inline virtual destructor to allow proper cleanup in derived classes. Does not perform framework-level teardown.
requirements: Ensure any resources owned by derived session types are released in their destructors.
Do not destroy a session while it might still be executing or being handled by the executor.

functions.name: Executor::init
functions.description: Initializes the Executor and its internal thread pool with the requested number of worker threads. Must be called before submitting sessions or adjusting thread counts.
requirements: Must be called before any other Executor methods (request(), increase_thread(), decrease_thread(), deinit()).
nthreads specifies the initial number of threads; valid range and minimum are unknown—callers must validate the return value for success/failure.
Should not be called multiple times without an intervening deinit().
Thread-safety of concurrent init() on the same instance is unknown; avoid concurrent calls.

functions.name: Executor::deinit
functions.description: Shuts down the Executor and its internal thread pool, releasing associated resources. Call when no further work will be submitted and active work is complete or has been cancelled by the framework.
requirements: Should only be called after a successful init().
Must not be called concurrently with request() or thread-count changes; ensure no in-flight operations require the executor or that the framework safely handles them (behavior unspecified).
After deinit(), the executor instance must not be used again unless re-initialized.

functions.name: Executor::request
functions.description: Submits an ExecSession to be executed by the Executor, associating it with the specified ExecQueue. The executor will invoke the session's virtual execute() and later handle(int state, int error) callbacks.
requirements: session must be a valid ExecSession instance with derived implementations of execute() and handle(int,int).
queue must refer to a valid, initialized ExecQueue (via ExecQueue::init()).
Executor must have been successfully initialized via init() prior to calling request().
Pointers session and queue must be non-null.
The lifetime of session and queue must extend at least until the executor finishes using them; destroying them prematurely may cause undefined behavior (exact completion criteria unknown).
Return value semantics are unknown; callers must check and handle the returned int appropriately.

functions.name: Executor::increase_thread
functions.description: Requests the executor to increase its worker thread count by one. Useful for scaling up processing capacity at runtime.
requirements: Executor must have been successfully initialized via init().
Effect on maximum thread limits, scheduling, and return value semantics are unknown; callers must check and handle the returned int.
Do not call after deinit().
Thread-safety of calling concurrently with other control methods is unknown.

functions.name: Executor::decrease_thread
functions.description: Requests the executor to decrease its worker thread count by one. Useful for scaling down processing capacity at runtime.
requirements: Executor must have been successfully initialized via init().
Behavior when the thread count would drop below a minimum is unknown; callers must check and handle the returned int.
Do not call after deinit().
Thread-safety of calling concurrently with other control methods is unknown.

functions.name: Executor::~Executor
functions.description: Destructor for Executor. Declared virtual and defined inline as empty; it does not perform shutdown. Use deinit() to stop threads and release resources.
requirements: Do not rely on the destructor to stop the thread pool or release resources; call deinit() explicitly before destruction.
Object must not be destroyed while other threads may still be running tasks managed by this executor.

functions.name: INIT_LIST_HEAD
functions.description: Initialize a circular doubly-linked list head so that it points to itself, representing an empty list. Typical usage: call once on a list_head before any add/remove operations.
requirements: list must be a valid, writable pointer to struct list_head
Should be called before the list_head is used with other list APIs
May be called to reinitialize a list head to the empty state

functions.name: __list_add
functions.signature: static inline void __list_add(struct list_head *entry, struct list_head *prev, struct list_head *next)
functions.description: Internal helper to insert entry between two known consecutive nodes prev and next in a circular doubly-linked list. Used when caller already has adjacent nodes for optimal code generation.
requirements: entry, prev, and next must be non-null valid pointers to nodes of the same list
prev and next must be adjacent (i.e., prev->next == next and next->prev == prev) before the call
entry must not currently be linked into any list (or must have been removed first)
The list must be in a consistent state (no concurrent modification)

functions.name: list_add
functions.signature: static inline void list_add(struct list_head *entry, struct list_head *head)
functions.description: Insert entry immediately after head in a circular doubly-linked list (push front). Commonly used to implement a stack (LIFO) on a list anchored by head.
requirements: entry and head must be non-null
head must be an initialized list head for the target list
entry must not currently be part of any list (remove it first if it is)
No concurrent modifications to the list during the operation

functions.name: list_add_tail
functions.signature: static inline void list_add_tail(struct list_head *entry, struct list_head *head)
functions.description: Insert entry immediately before head in a circular doubly-linked list (push back). Commonly used to implement a queue (FIFO).
requirements: entry and head must be non-null
head must be an initialized list head for the target list
entry must not currently be part of any list (remove it first if it is)
No concurrent modifications to the list during the operation

functions.name: __list_del
functions.signature: static inline void __list_del(struct list_head *prev, struct list_head *next)
functions.description: Internal helper to unlink a node by stitching together two nodes known to be adjacent in a circular doubly-linked list.
requirements: prev and next must be non-null
prev and next must be adjacent (i.e., prev->next is the node being removed and next->prev is the node being removed, so after removal they become neighbors)
Only use when the surrounding adjacency invariants are known to hold
No concurrent modifications during the operation

functions.name: list_del
functions.description: Remove entry from the circular doubly-linked list it is currently linked into. After deletion, entry’s next/prev are left in an undefined state and the node is not safe to use as a list head without reinitialization.
requirements: entry must be non-null
entry must currently be linked into a valid list (entry->prev and entry->next must be valid and consistent)
Do not rely on list_empty(entry) after deletion; entry is in an undefined state
No concurrent modifications to the list during the operation

functions.name: list_move
functions.signature: static inline void list_move(struct list_head *entry, struct list_head *head)
functions.description: Remove entry from its current list and insert it immediately after head (move to front of the destination list).
requirements: entry and head must be non-null
entry must currently be linked into some list
head must be an initialized list head of the destination list (can be the same list)
No concurrent modifications to the lists during the operation

functions.name: list_move_tail
functions.signature: static inline void list_move_tail(struct list_head *entry, struct list_head *head)
functions.description: Remove entry from its current list and insert it immediately before head (move to back of the destination list).
requirements: entry and head must be non-null
entry must currently be linked into some list
head must be an initialized list head of the destination list (can be the same list)
No concurrent modifications to the lists during the operation

functions.name: list_empty
functions.signature: static inline int list_empty(const struct list_head *head)
functions.description: Return nonzero if the circular doubly-linked list anchored at head is empty, zero otherwise.
requirements: head must be non-null and must be an initialized list head
Do not pass a standalone entry that is not an initialized list head

functions.name: __list_splice
functions.signature: static inline void __list_splice(const struct list_head *list, struct list_head *prev, struct list_head *next)
functions.description: Internal helper to splice (concatenate) all nodes from list into another list between adjacent nodes prev and next. Does not reinitialize list and assumes it is non-empty.
requirements: list, prev, and next must be non-null
list must be a valid, non-empty circular doubly-linked list (list->next and list->prev must not point to list itself)
prev and next must be adjacent nodes in the destination list (prev->next == next and next->prev == prev)
No concurrent modifications to either list during the operation

functions.name: list_splice
functions.signature: static inline void list_splice(const struct list_head *list, struct list_head *head)
functions.description: Splice all elements from list into the destination list immediately after head. If list is empty, does nothing. The source list head is not reinitialized; its elements are transferred but list remains a valid (now-empty) head only if it was empty to begin with.
requirements: list and head must be non-null
Both list and head must be initialized list heads of circular doubly-linked lists
Safe to call when list is empty; no effect in that case
No concurrent modifications to either list during the operation

functions.name: list_splice_init
functions.signature: static inline void list_splice_init(struct list_head *list, struct list_head *head)
functions.description: Splice all elements from list into the destination list immediately after head, then reinitialize list to the empty state. Useful for moving all elements while leaving the source list reusable.
requirements: list and head must be non-null
Both list and head must be initialized list heads of circular doubly-linked lists
If list is empty, function does nothing aside from leaving list initialized
No concurrent modifications to either list during the operation

functions.name: INIT_SLIST_HEAD
functions.description: Initialize a singly linked list head to represent an empty list. Sets first.next to NULL and last to point to the first sentinel.
requirements: list must be a valid, writable pointer to struct slist_head
Should be called before the list is used

functions.name: slist_add_after
functions.signature: static inline void slist_add_after(struct slist_node *entry, struct slist_node *prev, struct slist_head *list)
functions.description: Insert entry after the node prev within the singly linked list identified by list. Updates tail pointer if appending at the end.
requirements: entry, prev, and list must be non-null
prev must be a node that belongs to the given list
entry must not currently be part of any singly linked list (its next is ignored and overwritten)
No concurrent modifications to the list during the operation

functions.name: slist_add_head
functions.signature: static inline void slist_add_head(struct slist_node *entry, struct slist_head *list)
functions.description: Insert entry at the head (front) of the singly linked list. Internally inserts after the sentinel first node.
requirements: entry and list must be non-null
list must be an initialized slist_head
entry must not currently be part of any singly linked list
No concurrent modifications to the list during the operation

functions.name: slist_add_tail
functions.signature: static inline void slist_add_tail(struct slist_node *entry, struct slist_head *list)
functions.description: Append entry to the tail (back) of the singly linked list. Efficiently updates the tail pointer.
requirements: entry and list must be non-null
list must be an initialized slist_head
entry must not currently be part of any singly linked list
No concurrent modifications to the list during the operation

functions.name: slist_del_after
functions.signature: static inline void slist_del_after(struct slist_node *prev, struct slist_head *list)
functions.description: Delete the node immediately following prev in the singly linked list, updating the tail pointer if the last element is removed.
requirements: prev and list must be non-null
prev must be a node that belongs to the given list
prev->next must be non-null (there must be a node to delete)
No concurrent modifications to the list during the operation

functions.name: slist_del_head
functions.description: Remove the first element (head element) from the singly linked list.
requirements: list must be non-null and initialized
The list must not be empty (list->first.next must be non-null)
No concurrent modifications to the list during the operation

functions.name: slist_empty
functions.signature: static inline int slist_empty(const struct slist_head *list)
functions.description: Return nonzero if the singly linked list is empty, zero otherwise.
requirements: list must be non-null and initialized

functions.name: __slist_splice
functions.signature: static inline void __slist_splice(const struct slist_head *list, struct slist_node *prev, struct slist_head *head)
functions.description: Internal helper to splice all nodes from list into another singly linked list after prev. Updates the destination tail if needed. The source list is not reinitialized.
requirements: list, prev, and head must be non-null
list must be a valid, non-empty singly linked list
prev must be a node in the destination list identified by head
No concurrent modifications to either list during the operation

functions.name: slist_splice
functions.signature: static inline void slist_splice(const struct slist_head *list, struct slist_node *prev, struct slist_head *head)
functions.description: Splice all nodes from list into the destination singly linked list after prev. If list is empty, does nothing. The source list head is unchanged and not reinitialized.
requirements: list, prev, and head must be non-null
Both list and head must be initialized singly linked lists
Safe to call when list is empty; no effect in that case
prev must be a node in the destination list identified by head
No concurrent modifications to either list during the operation

functions.name: slist_splice_init
functions.signature: static inline void slist_splice_init(struct slist_head *list, struct slist_node *prev, struct slist_head *head)
functions.description: Splice all nodes from list into the destination singly linked list after prev, then reinitialize list to empty. Useful for moving all elements while keeping the source reusable.
requirements: list, prev, and head must be non-null
Both list and head must be initialized singly linked lists
If list is empty, function does nothing aside from leaving list initialized
prev must be a node in the destination list identified by head
No concurrent modifications to either list during the operation

functions.name: mpoller_create
functions.description: Create a multi-poller instance wrapping multiple underlying pollers. The instance distributes operations across nthreads underlying pollers. Typical usage: allocate once at startup, then start it, set the callback, and add fds/timers. Details such as allocation failures and parameter validation are not documented in this header.
requirements: params may be NULL or point to a valid struct poller_params; exact fields and constraints are defined in poller.h (unknown here).
nthreads should be greater than 0; behavior for 0 is unspecified.
Must be called before any other mpoller_* functions that take an mpoller_t*.
Return value must be checked by the caller before use; NULL handling policy is unknown but should be assumed possible.

functions.name: mpoller_start
functions.description: Start the multi-poller, typically creating/running its worker threads and beginning event processing. Call after successful creation (and optionally after setting the callback) and before adding fds/timers if required by the underlying implementation.
requirements: mpoller must be a valid pointer returned by mpoller_create and not yet destroyed.
May be called at most once prior to stop/destroy; repeated calls behavior is unspecified.
Return value is an int; success/failure semantics are unspecified (check for nonzero/zero per underlying implementation).

functions.name: mpoller_set_callback
functions.description: Set the event callback invoked by the pollers when events are delivered. The callback receives a pointer to a poller_result and a user-provided context pointer (source and lifetime of the context are defined by the underlying poller). Should be set before starting or before events are generated.
requirements: callback must be a valid function pointer with signature void(struct poller_result *, void *).
The callback must be safe to be called from multiple threads concurrently, as events may be delivered on different poller threads.
mpoller must be a valid pointer returned by mpoller_create and not yet destroyed.
Must be called before events are processed; exact timing constraints relative to mpoller_start are unspecified.

functions.name: mpoller_stop
functions.description: Stop the multi-poller, typically signaling worker threads to exit and halting event processing. Use during shutdown before destroying the multi-poller.
requirements: mpoller must be a valid pointer returned by mpoller_create and not yet destroyed.
Should be called before mpoller_destroy; calling after destroy is invalid.
Thread-safety and whether it blocks until threads exit are unspecified.

functions.name: mpoller_destroy
functions.description: Destroy and free resources associated with a multi-poller instance. Should be called once after stopping to avoid leaks. After this call, the mpoller pointer must not be used.
requirements: mpoller must be a valid pointer returned by mpoller_create and not used after destruction.
All outstanding operations (fds/timers) should be cleaned up or stopped beforehand; exact requirements are unspecified.
Typically called after mpoller_stop; destroying a running poller has unspecified behavior.

functions.name: mpoller_add
functions.signature: static inline int mpoller_add(const struct poller_data *data, int timeout, mpoller_t *mpoller);
functions.description: Add a file descriptor/event to the multi-poller. The target underlying poller is selected as (unsigned)data->fd % mpoller->nthreads. This forwards to poller_add for that shard.
requirements: mpoller must be a valid, started multi-poller with nthreads > 0.
data must be non-NULL and point to a valid struct poller_data; its fd field must be a non-negative file descriptor suitable for polling.
timeout is forwarded to poller_add; its units/valid range are unspecified here.
Return value propagates from poller_add; success/failure semantics are defined by poller_add (unknown here).

functions.name: mpoller_del
functions.signature: static inline int mpoller_del(int fd, mpoller_t *mpoller);
functions.description: Delete/unregister a file descriptor from the multi-poller. The shard is chosen by (unsigned)fd % mpoller->nthreads and the call is forwarded to poller_del on that shard.
requirements: mpoller must be a valid, started multi-poller with nthreads > 0.
fd must be a non-negative file descriptor that was previously added to this mpoller.
Return value is that of poller_del; exact semantics are unspecified here.

functions.name: mpoller_mod
functions.signature: static inline int mpoller_mod(const struct poller_data *data, int timeout, mpoller_t *mpoller);
functions.description: Modify an existing registration for a file descriptor in the multi-poller, forwarding to poller_mod on the shard selected by (unsigned)data->fd % nthreads.
requirements: mpoller must be a valid, started multi-poller with nthreads > 0.
data must be non-NULL and reference a previously added file descriptor via its fd field; fd must be non-negative.
timeout is forwarded to poller_mod; units/valid range are unspecified here.
Return value is that of poller_mod; exact semantics are unspecified.

functions.name: mpoller_set_timeout
functions.signature: static inline int mpoller_set_timeout(int fd, int timeout, mpoller_t *mpoller);
functions.description: Adjust the timeout for an already-registered file descriptor, forwarding to poller_set_timeout on the shard selected by (unsigned)fd % nthreads.
requirements: mpoller must be a valid, started multi-poller with nthreads > 0.
fd must be a non-negative file descriptor already known to the mpoller.
timeout semantics (units/range) are unspecified here and are defined by poller_set_timeout.
Return value is that of poller_set_timeout; exact semantics are unspecified.

functions.name: mpoller_add_timer
functions.signature: static inline int mpoller_add_timer(const struct timespec *value, void *context, void **timer, int *index, mpoller_t *mpoller);
functions.description: Add a timer to the multi-poller. The function selects a shard in round-robin fashion, stores the selected index in *index, and forwards to poller_add_timer on that shard. The created timer handle is returned via *timer.
requirements: mpoller must be a valid, started multi-poller with nthreads > 0.
value must be non-NULL and point to a valid timespec specifying the timer interval/expiration; exact semantics are defined by poller_add_timer (unknown here).
timer must be non-NULL and point to storage for receiving an opaque timer handle.
index must be non-NULL; on success it receives the shard index that must be used when deleting the timer.
context is an opaque user pointer passed to the callback; may be NULL.
Return value is that of poller_add_timer; exact semantics are unspecified.

functions.name: mpoller_del_timer
functions.signature: static inline int mpoller_del_timer(void *timer, int index, mpoller_t *mpoller);
functions.description: Delete/cancel a timer previously added with mpoller_add_timer. The caller must provide the same shard index returned by mpoller_add_timer via *index so the timer is removed from the correct underlying poller.
requirements: mpoller must be a valid, started multi-poller with nthreads > 0.
timer must be a valid timer handle previously returned by mpoller_add_timer.
index must be the exact shard index returned by mpoller_add_timer for this timer; using an incorrect index may fail or target the wrong poller.
Return value is that of poller_del_timer; exact semantics are unspecified.

functions.name: poller_create
functions.description: Create and initialize a new poller instance. Typical usage is to fill a poller_params structure with an optional max_open_files limit, a completion callback, and a user context, then pass it here to obtain a poller handle for subsequent operations (start/add/mod/del/stop/destroy). Details about parameter validation and defaults are not documented in this header; behavior when params is NULL is unknown.
requirements: params: if provided, its callback (if non-NULL) must be callable with (struct poller_result *, void *).
The returned poller_t* must be passed to other poller_* APIs of this interface.
Thread-safety and lifetime requirements of params->context are unknown; it should remain valid while callbacks may occur.

functions.name: poller_start
functions.description: Start the poller’s event loop/processing so that added operations (I/O, timers, etc.) can be serviced and callbacks invoked. Intended to be called after poller_create and before adding operations, or at least before expecting them to run. Run/dispatch semantics (blocking vs. nonblocking, threading) are not specified here.
requirements: poller must be a valid pointer returned by poller_create and not yet destroyed.
May only be called on a properly initialized poller; re-entrancy or multiple calls semantics are unknown.

functions.name: poller_add
functions.signature: int poller_add(const struct poller_data *data, int timeout, poller_t *poller);
functions.description: Register an operation with the poller (read/write/connect/listen/SSL operations, recvfrom, timer via PD_OP_TIMER, event/notify, etc.) as described by poller_data. The timeout applies to this operation. Exact timeout units and semantics are not documented in this header.
requirements: poller must be a valid poller_t* from poller_create.

data must point to a properly initialized poller_data with operation set to one of PD_OP_* constants and required fields for that operation filled (e.g., fd for socket operations, ssl for SSL operations, appropriate callback union member and context as needed).
timeout must be a valid integer per library expectations; units/allowed ranges are unknown.
Pointers embedded in data (e.g., callbacks, message, write_iov, context) must remain valid until the operation completes or is cancelled.

functions.name: poller_del
functions.description: Remove/unregister the operation(s) associated with the given file descriptor from the poller.
requirements: poller must be a valid poller_t* from poller_create.
fd must be a valid file descriptor that was previously added to this poller via poller_add/poller_mod.
Effect on multiple operations bound to the same fd, if any, is unspecified here.

functions.name: poller_mod
functions.signature: int poller_mod(const struct poller_data *data, int timeout, poller_t *poller);
functions.description: Modify an existing registration on the poller, updating the operation and/or parameters as specified by poller_data, and optionally its timeout.
requirements: poller must be a valid poller_t* from poller_create.
data must describe an already-registered target (e.g., via matching fd) and be initialized consistently with the intended PD_OP_* operation.
timeout must be valid per library expectations; units/allowed ranges are unknown.
Pointers embedded in data must remain valid for the duration of the modified operation.

functions.name: poller_set_timeout
functions.signature: int poller_set_timeout(int fd, int timeout, poller_t *poller);
functions.description: Update the timeout for the operation(s) associated with a given file descriptor within the poller. Exact timeout units are not specified here.
requirements: poller must be a valid poller_t* from poller_create.
fd must refer to an operation previously added to this poller.
timeout must be a valid integer per library expectations; units/allowed ranges are unknown.

functions.name: poller_add_timer
functions.signature: int poller_add_timer(const struct timespec *value, void *context, void **timer, poller_t *poller);
functions.description: Schedule a timer event to fire after the interval specified by value. On success, stores an opaque handle to the created timer in *timer. When the timer triggers, the poller’s callback will receive a poller_result with PD_OP_TIMER and the supplied context. Exact firing semantics (one-shot vs. periodic) are not stated in this header.
requirements: poller must be a valid poller_t* from poller_create.
value must point to a valid timespec specifying the timer interval; interpretation (relative/absolute) is not documented here.
timer must be a valid non-NULL pointer to receive the created timer handle.
context should remain valid until the timer fires or is cancelled.

functions.name: poller_del_timer
functions.description: Cancel and remove a previously added timer identified by the opaque timer handle returned via poller_add_timer.
requirements: poller must be a valid poller_t* from poller_create.
timer must be a valid handle previously returned by poller_add_timer for this poller.

functions.name: poller_set_callback
functions.description: Set or replace the poller’s result callback, which is invoked for completion/status updates for registered operations. This can override the callback provided in poller_params at creation time.
requirements: poller must be a valid poller_t* from poller_create.
callback, if non-NULL, must be callable with (struct poller_result *, void *). Whether NULL is allowed to disable callbacks is not specified.
The callback must be re-entrant/thread-safe if the implementation may invoke it from worker threads; threading model is unknown.

functions.name: poller_stop
functions.description: Request the poller to stop processing events. Use before destroying the poller or when shutting down. Stop semantics (synchronous vs. asynchronous) are not specified here.
requirements: poller must be a valid poller_t* from poller_create.
Should be called before poller_destroy to ensure orderly shutdown; exact ordering requirements are not specified.

functions.name: poller_destroy
functions.description: Destroy and free resources associated with a poller created by poller_create. Typically called after stopping the poller and ensuring no further callbacks will occur.
requirements: poller must be a valid poller_t* previously returned by poller_create and not used after destruction.
It is the caller’s responsibility to ensure outstanding operations are stopped/cancelled prior to destruction; exact requirements are not specified.

functions.name: msgqueue_create
functions.description: Creates a new simple message queue. The queue can operate in blocking or nonblocking mode (switchable via msgqueue_set_block/msgqueue_set_nonblock). In blocking mode, the number of pending messages may grow up to twice maxlen; in nonblocking mode it is unbounded. linkoff specifies, relative to the start of each message object, the byte offset to a writable pointer-sized storage used internally for linking. linkoff may be negative, zero, or positive. Usage: call to obtain a queue handle, then pass that handle to get/put functions.
requirements: maxlen: capacity hint for blocking mode; in blocking mode pending messages may reach up to 2 * maxlen (explicitly documented)
linkoff: for each message object you enqueue, there must be writable storage of at least sizeof(void*) at address (char*)msg + linkoff for internal linkage (explicitly documented)
linkoff may be negative, zero, or positive (explicitly documented)
The returned msgqueue_t* must be checked for NULL if the implementation can fail to allocate (not specified; failure mode unknown)
The queue handle must be destroyed with msgqueue_destroy when no longer needed
Thread-safety, error reporting, and constraints on maxlen values are not documented; behavior for maxlen == 0 is unknown

functions.name: msgqueue_get
functions.description: Dequeues and returns the next message from the queue. In blocking mode, this likely blocks when the queue is empty; in nonblocking mode, it likely returns immediately (possibly with NULL) when empty. Usage: call to retrieve messages previously enqueued via msgqueue_put or msgqueue_put_head.
requirements: queue must be a valid pointer returned by msgqueue_create and not yet destroyed
In blocking mode, the call may block if the queue is empty (inferred from documented blocking/nonblocking modes)
In nonblocking mode, pending messages are unbounded; behavior on empty (e.g., returning NULL) is not explicitly documented and is unknown
Returned pointer is the original msg pointer supplied to put; caller owns any further handling or deallocation (ownership semantics beyond retrieval are not documented)

functions.name: msgqueue_put
functions.description: Enqueues a message at the tail of the queue. In blocking mode, this may block under internal capacity limits; in nonblocking mode, the queue grows without bound. The message object must provide pointer-sized storage at the configured linkoff for internal linkage.
requirements: queue must be a valid pointer returned by msgqueue_create and not yet destroyed
msg must be a valid pointer to a message object whose memory remains valid until the message is dequeued
At address (char*)msg + linkoff (specified at queue creation), there must be writable storage of at least sizeof(void*) for internal use (explicitly documented)
In blocking mode, the call may block; pending messages may reach up to 2 * maxlen (explicitly documented)
In nonblocking mode, the call should not block; pending messages are unbounded (explicitly documented)
Thread-safety, error returns, and behavior on NULL msg are not documented and thus unknown

functions.name: msgqueue_put_head
functions.description: Enqueues a message at the head of the queue (priority insertion before existing items). Semantics mirror msgqueue_put regarding blocking vs nonblocking modes and the linkoff requirement.
requirements: queue must be a valid pointer returned by msgqueue_create and not yet destroyed
msg must be a valid pointer to a message object whose memory remains valid until the message is dequeued
At address (char*)msg + linkoff (specified at queue creation), there must be writable storage of at least sizeof(void*) for internal use (explicitly documented)
In blocking mode, the call may block; pending messages may reach up to 2 * maxlen (explicitly documented)
In nonblocking mode, the call should not block; pending messages are unbounded (explicitly documented)
Exact ordering guarantees beyond head insertion are not documented

functions.name: msgqueue_set_nonblock
functions.description: Switches the queue to nonblocking mode, in which pending messages can grow without bound and queue operations should not block. Use when producers/consumers must not block.
requirements: queue must be a valid pointer returned by msgqueue_create and not yet destroyed
After switching to nonblocking mode, pending messages are unbounded in size (explicitly documented); callers must ensure this is acceptable for memory usage
Thread-safety and whether it is safe to change mode concurrently with get/put operations are not documented and thus unknown

functions.name: msgqueue_set_block
functions.description: Switches the queue to blocking mode, where operations may block under internal capacity limits. In this mode, the number of pending messages may reach up to twice the maxlen specified at creation.
requirements: queue must be a valid pointer returned by msgqueue_create and not yet destroyed
In blocking mode, callers must tolerate potential blocking in get/put operations (inferred from mode)
Pending messages may grow up to 2 * maxlen in blocking mode (explicitly documented)
Thread-safety and whether it is safe to change mode concurrently with get/put operations are not documented and thus unknown

functions.name: msgqueue_destroy
functions.description: Destroys the message queue and releases its internal resources. After this call, the queue handle must not be used. The fate of any messages still in the queue is not documented.
requirements: queue must be a valid pointer previously returned by msgqueue_create
The queue handle must not be used after destruction

Behavior if there are still pending messages at destroy time is not documented; callers should ensure they have drained the queue or otherwise accounted for message ownership before destroying (ownership semantics unknown)
Thread-safety and whether it is safe to destroy while other threads are operating on the queue are not documented

functions.name: rb_insert_color
functions.description: Rebalances and recolors a red-black tree after you have inserted a new node as a red leaf. Typical usage: first place node into the tree in key order using rb_link_node(), then call rb_insert_color(node, root) to restore red-black properties.
requirements: node must already be linked into the tree as a red leaf via rb_link_node() at the correct parent/link position
root must be a valid rb_root for the tree containing node
The key/order relationship must be satisfied by the caller when choosing the insertion position

functions.name: rb_erase
functions.description: Removes a node from a red-black tree and rebalances the tree as needed to maintain red-black invariants.
requirements: node must be currently present in the tree identified by root
root must be a valid rb_root
After removal, any pointers stored in node are no longer valid for tree operations and should not be reused without reinitialization

functions.name: rb_next
functions.description: Returns the in-order successor of the given node within its red-black tree, or NULL if the node is the last element.
requirements: The input node pointer must refer to a node that is part of a valid red-black tree
Returns NULL if there is no successor; callers must handle a NULL return

functions.name: rb_prev
functions.description: Returns the in-order predecessor of the given node within its red-black tree, or NULL if the node is the first element.
requirements: The input node pointer must refer to a node that is part of a valid red-black tree
Returns NULL if there is no predecessor; callers must handle a NULL return

functions.name: rb_first
functions.description: Returns the leftmost (minimum key) node in the given red-black tree root, or NULL if the tree is empty.
requirements: root must be a valid rb_root (may be empty)
Returns NULL if the tree is empty; callers must handle a NULL return

functions.name: rb_last
functions.description: Returns the rightmost (maximum key) node in the given red-black tree root, or NULL if the tree is empty.
requirements: root must be a valid rb_root (may be empty)
Returns NULL if the tree is empty; callers must handle a NULL return

functions.name: rb_replace_node
functions.signature: void rb_replace_node(struct rb_node *victim, struct rb_node *newnode, struct rb_root *root);
functions.description: Replaces one node in a red-black tree with another node without performing a remove+rebalance followed by an insert+rebalance. Intended for in-place key-preserving replacement.
requirements: victim must be currently present in the tree identified by root
newnode must not be part of any tree at the time of replacement
The replacement must preserve the tree’s ordering (i.e., the key represented by newnode must be equivalent to the victim’s key)
root must be a valid rb_root

functions.name: rb_link_node
functions.signature: static inline void rb_link_node(struct rb_node *node, struct rb_node *parent, struct rb_node **link);
functions.description: Initializes and links a node as a red leaf under the specified parent at the given child link location. This performs the structural insertion only; callers must later call rb_insert_color() to rebalance.
requirements: parent is either NULL (for inserting at the root) or a valid node in the destination tree
link must point to the parent’s appropriate child pointer (either &parent->rb_left or &parent->rb_right) or, if parent is NULL, to &root->rb_node maintained by the caller
node must not currently be linked into any tree
After rb_link_node, callers should call rb_insert_color(node, root) to restore red-black invariants

functions.name: SubTask::dispatch
functions.description: Entry point to execute a SubTask. This is a pure virtual method that must be implemented by subclasses to perform the unit of work associated with the task. Typical usage is to implement this in derived classes and trigger the task through the framework that manages SubTask instances. Further coordination behavior is unknown from this header.
requirements: Must be overridden in any concrete subclass; SubTask cannot be instantiated directly.
No parameters and no return value; any completion signaling mechanism is not defined here (unknown).

functions.name: SubTask::subtask_done
functions.description: Marks a SubTask as finished. Intended to be called by the task implementation when its work completes, likely to notify the framework and/or its parent ParallelTask. Actual side effects are not visible here; details are unknown.
requirements: Protected method: can only be called from within SubTask or its derived classes.
Should be invoked by the task implementation upon completion; exact call timing and frequency are not specified in this header (unknown).

functions.name: SubTask::get_pointer
functions.description: Returns the opaque user pointer associated with this SubTask. Useful for attaching and retrieving user-defined context without imposing a type.
requirements: Safe to call on a const SubTask instance.
Returns the pointer previously set via set_pointer or NULL if none was set.

functions.name: SubTask::set_pointer
functions.description: Associates an opaque user pointer with this SubTask. The class neither allocates nor frees this pointer; it is a simple storage for user context.
requirements: pointer may be NULL or any valid pointer value; ownership and lifetime management are the caller’s responsibility (no ownership semantics are defined here).

functions.name: SubTask::SubTask
functions.description: Default constructor for SubTask. Initializes internal fields, including parent and user pointer, to NULL. As SubTask is abstract, this is used by derived classes.
requirements: SubTask is abstract due to a pure virtual dispatch; only derived classes can be instantiated.

functions.name: SubTask::~SubTask
functions.description: Virtual destructor for SubTask. Enables safe destruction via base-class pointers. Inline and empty in this header.
requirements: No special requirements; ensures proper cleanup in derived classes via virtual dispatch.

functions.name: ParallelTask::dispatch
functions.description: Executes the ParallelTask. Expected to manage and/or dispatch its array of subtasks, coordinating their execution. Exact scheduling, concurrency, and completion semantics are not specified in this header (unknown).
requirements: ParallelTask must have been constructed with a subtasks array and count.
Behavior depends on internal framework; no parameters and no explicit error reporting are defined here.

functions.name: ParallelTask::ParallelTask
functions.description: Constructs a ParallelTask over an array of SubTask pointers. Stores the array pointer and the number of subtasks; does not copy or allocate subtasks.
requirements: subtasks must point to an array of at least n elements (SubTask*).
The subtasks array pointer must remain valid for the lifetime of the ParallelTask instance, as it is stored directly.
n is the number of elements in the subtasks array; must accurately reflect the array size.

functions.name: ParallelTask::~ParallelTask
functions.description: Virtual destructor for ParallelTask. Allows safe deletion through base-class pointers. Inline and empty in this header; does not imply ownership of the subtasks array or elements.
requirements: No special requirements; does not indicate ownership transfer of subtasks or their array in this header (unknown).

functions.name: thrdpool_create
functions.description: Creates a thread pool object with a specified number of worker threads and per-thread stack size. Typical usage: call this once to obtain a pool handle, then submit tasks to it and eventually destroy the pool when no longer needed. Detailed behavior (return value semantics, exact constraints on nthreads/stacksize) is not documented in the header and remains unknown.
requirements: The returned thrdpool_t* must be passed to thrdpool_destroy to release resources (inferred from naming/lifecycle patterns).
Inputs nthreads and stacksize should be sensible values for thread creation; exact valid ranges are unknown from the header.
Do not use the returned pointer after it has been destroyed.

functions.name: thrdpool_schedule
functions.description: Schedules a task for execution on the specified thread pool. The task carries a function pointer (routine) and an opaque context pointer passed to that routine. Return value semantics are not specified in the header; typically nonzero indicates an error, but exact meanings are unknown.
requirements: pool must be a valid thread pool created by thrdpool_create and not yet destroyed.
task must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to a struct thrdpool_task.
task->routine must be a valid function pointer compatible with void (*)(void*).
task->context must be valid for use by task->routine for the lifetime required by execution (exact lifetime management is unknown).
Caller should not modify or free resources required by the task before it is executed; exact ownership semantics are unknown.

functions.name: thrdpool_in_pool
functions.description: Returns an integer indicating whether the calling thread is part of the specified thread pool (inferred from name). Exact return value conventions (e.g., 1/0, positive/negative) are not documented and remain unknown.
requirements: pool must be a valid thread pool created by thrdpool_create and not yet destroyed.

functions.name: thrdpool_increase
functions.description: Requests an increase of the number of worker threads in the pool (inferred from name). The amount increased and return value semantics are not specified in the header and remain unknown.
requirements: pool must be a valid thread pool created by thrdpool_create and not yet destroyed.
Caller should handle the return value to detect failure or inability to increase, but exact conventions are unknown.

functions.name: thrdpool_decrease
functions.description: Requests a decrease of the number of worker threads in the pool (inferred from name). How many threads are decreased and return value semantics are not specified in the header and remain unknown.
requirements: pool must be a valid thread pool created by thrdpool_create and not yet destroyed.
Caller should handle the return value to detect failure or inability to decrease, but exact conventions are unknown.

functions.name: thrdpool_exit
functions.description: Signals that the calling thread should exit from the specified thread pool (inferred from name). Intended usage is likely from within a worker executing in the pool; precise semantics are not documented and remain unknown.
requirements: pool must be a valid thread pool created by thrdpool_create and not yet destroyed.
Should be called from a thread that is part of the given pool (inferred from name and typical patterns).
Effects on in-flight tasks or scheduling are unknown; callers should ensure this aligns with their concurrency model.

functions.name: thrdpool_destroy
functions.description: Destroys the thread pool and releases its resources. A callback may be provided to receive notification of tasks that remain pending at destruction time; it accepts a pointer to each pending thrdpool_task. Exact destruction order and whether the callback is optional are not specified and remain unknown.
requirements: pool must be a valid thread pool created by thrdpool_create.
Must be called exactly once for each successfully created pool to avoid resource leaks (inferred from lifecycle patterns).

pending must be a valid function pointer if provided; it must be safe to call for each pending task and must not assume task memory ownership unless documented elsewhere. Whether pending can be NULL is unknown.
After destruction returns, the pool pointer must not be used again.

functions.name: IOSession::prep_pread
functions.signature: void IOSession::prep_pread(int fd, void *buf, size_t count, long long offset);
functions.description: Prepares this IOSession for an asynchronous positioned read (pread) operation using Linux AIO (iocb). Intended to be called from a subclass’s prepare() implementation to set up the request before submission by IOService. The actual I/O is completed later and its result can be obtained via get_res() inside handle().
requirements: Must be invoked from within the overriding IOSession::prepare() before the session is submitted.
fd must be a valid open file descriptor supporting positioned reads.
buf must point to a writable buffer of at least count bytes for the data to be read.
count should be the number of bytes to read (0 is typically a no-op; exact behavior depends on the underlying system).
offset should be a non-negative file offset for the positioned read.
Do not free or modify the buffer until the operation completes and handle() is invoked.

functions.name: IOSession::prep_pwrite
functions.signature: void IOSession::prep_pwrite(int fd, void *buf, size_t count, long long offset);
functions.description: Prepares this IOSession for an asynchronous positioned write (pwrite) operation using Linux AIO. To be called by a subclass in prepare() prior to submission by IOService. Completion status/bytes written will be available via get_res() in handle().
requirements: Must be invoked from within the overriding IOSession::prepare() before the session is submitted.
fd must be a valid open file descriptor supporting positioned writes.
buf must point to a readable buffer of at least count bytes containing the data to write.
count should be the number of bytes to write (0 may be a no-op; depends on system).
offset should be a non-negative file offset for the positioned write.
Do not free or modify the buffer contents until the operation completes and handle() is invoked.

functions.name: IOSession::prep_preadv
functions.signature: void IOSession::prep_preadv(int fd, const struct iovec *iov, int iovcnt, long long offset);
functions.description: Prepares this IOSession for an asynchronous vectored positioned read (preadv) using Linux AIO. Call from prepare() to set up the iocb for multiple buffers; IOService submits it. Use get_res() in handle() to obtain the result (bytes read or error).
requirements: Must be invoked from within the overriding IOSession::prepare() before the session is submitted.
fd must be a valid open file descriptor supporting positioned reads.
iov must point to an array of iovec entries describing writable destination buffers.
Each iovec base pointer must be valid and the buffers large enough for the requested transfer.
iovcnt must be greater than 0 and within system limits for preadv.
offset should be a non-negative file offset for the positioned read.
The iovec array and its buffers must remain valid until the operation completes and handle() is invoked.

functions.name: IOSession::prep_pwritev
functions.signature: void IOSession::prep_pwritev(int fd, const struct iovec *iov, int iovcnt, long long offset);
functions.description: Prepares this IOSession for an asynchronous vectored positioned write (pwritev) using Linux AIO. Call from prepare() to set up a write of multiple buffers; IOService submits it. Use get_res() in handle() to obtain completion status/bytes written.
requirements: Must be invoked from within the overriding IOSession::prepare() before the session is submitted.
fd must be a valid open file descriptor supporting positioned writes.
iov must point to an array of iovec entries describing readable source buffers.
Each iovec base pointer must be valid and contain at least the number of bytes specified in the iovec length.
iovcnt must be greater than 0 and within system limits for pwritev.
offset should be a non-negative file offset for the positioned write.
The iovec array and its buffers must remain valid until the operation completes and handle() is invoked.

functions.name: IOSession::prep_fsync
functions.description: Prepares this IOSession for an asynchronous fsync operation on the given file descriptor using Linux AIO. Call from prepare(); IOService will submit it. Use get_res() in handle() to read the completion status.
requirements: Must be invoked from within the overriding IOSession::prepare() before the session is submitted.
fd must be a valid open file descriptor for which fsync is supported.
Underlying file must remain open until the operation completes.

functions.name: IOSession::prep_fdatasync
functions.description: Prepares this IOSession for an asynchronous fdatasync operation on the given file descriptor using Linux AIO. Call from prepare(); IOService will submit it. Use get_res() in handle() to obtain completion status.
requirements: Must be invoked from within the overriding IOSession::prepare() before the session is submitted.
fd must be a valid open file descriptor for which fdatasync is supported.
Underlying file must remain open until the operation completes.

functions.name: IOSession::get_res
functions.description: Returns the result of the completed asynchronous operation associated with this IOSession. Typically represents the number of bytes transferred or a negative error code, but the exact convention is not documented here. Intended for use in handle().
requirements: Call only after the operation has completed (e.g., within or after handle()).
Interpretation of the return value (bytes vs. error) is library-defined and not documented in this header; callers must handle unknown conventions safely.

functions.name: IOService::init
functions.description: Initializes the IOService and its underlying Linux AIO context and event notification mechanism. Must be called before submitting any IOSession via request(). Return value semantics are not documented in this header.
requirements: Must be called before any other IOService operation (such as request or deinit).
maxevents should be a positive integer appropriate for the event processing capacity; exact constraints are not specified.
Must not be called multiple times without an intervening deinit.

functions.name: IOService::deinit
functions.description: Shuts down the IOService, releasing its AIO context, eventfd, and any related resources. Use to clean up after init() when the service is no longer needed.
requirements: Should be called after a successful init().
Must not be called concurrently with request() or while operations are still being initialized; exact concurrency guarantees are not documented.
Do not use the IOService for further requests after deinit().

functions.name: IOService::request
functions.description: Submits an IOSession to the IOService for asynchronous execution. The session’s prepare() is expected to set up the operation (via a prep_ method), and completion will be delivered to the session’s handle().
requirements: session must be non-null.
session must be a valid IOSession instance whose prepare() sets exactly one operation using a prep_ method as hinted by the comment in IOSession.
IOService must have been successfully initialized via init() prior to calling request().
The IOSession object must remain alive until its handle() is invoked (lifetime management is required).
Return value/error semantics are not documented in this header; callers should check and handle non-zero/negative returns defensively.

functions.name: IOService::create_event_fd
functions.description: Factory method to create the event file descriptor used by IOService for notifications. The default implementation returns eventfd(0, 0). Can be overridden by subclasses to customize eventfd creation flags or mechanism.
requirements: If overridden, the method should return a valid file descriptor on success or a suitable error indicator on failure consistent with IOService::init() expectations.
No direct caller requirements; used internally by IOService::init().

functions.name: IOService::~IOService
functions.description: Virtual destructor for IOService. Ensures proper cleanup through deinit() patterns when deleted via a base pointer. The body is empty in this header; resource release is expected to be handled by deinit().
requirements: Before destruction, deinit() should be called to release resources; not enforced by the destructor per this header.

functions.name: IOSession::~IOSession
functions.description: Virtual destructor for IOSession, allowing deletion via base-class pointers. No additional behavior is defined in this header.
requirements: Ensure any in-flight asynchronous operations associated with the session are complete or canceled before destroying the object; not enforced by the destructor per this header.

functions.name: protocol::ProtocolMessage::set_size_limit
functions.description: Sets the maximum allowed size (in bytes) for the message. Typically used by decoders/parsers to cap how much data may be accepted or processed.
requirements: limit is a byte count; use (size_t)-1 to indicate no limit (the default).
Caller should choose a value appropriate for the protocol to avoid truncation or rejection in custom append/encode implementations.

functions.name: protocol::ProtocolMessage::get_size_limit
functions.description: Returns the current maximum allowed size (in bytes) for the message.

functions.name: protocol::ProtocolMessage::set_attachment
functions.description: Associates an Attachment object with the message. ProtocolMessage deletes its Attachment in the destructor, implying ownership is transferred to the message.
requirements: att may be null.
Ownership of att is assumed by ProtocolMessage; it will be deleted in ~ProtocolMessage.
If replacing an existing attachment, the caller must ensure the previous attachment has been deleted or was null (set_attachment does not delete or manage the previous pointer).
Attachment must be allocated with an operator compatible with delete (i.e., new).

functions.name: protocol::ProtocolMessage::get_attachment
functions.description: Returns the mutable pointer to the associated Attachment owned by this message, or null if none.
requirements: Do not delete the returned pointer; it is owned and deleted by ProtocolMessage.
Pointer remains valid until it is replaced via set_attachment, the message is moved-from (which transfers it), or the message is destroyed.

functions.name: protocol::ProtocolMessage::ProtocolMessage
functions.description: Default constructor. Initializes size_limit to no limit ((size_t)-1), attachment to null, and wrapper to null.

functions.name: protocol::ProtocolMessage::ProtocolMessage
functions.description: Move constructor. Transfers size_limit and the owned Attachment from the source; sets the source's attachment to null. The wrapper pointer is reset to null in the new object.
requirements: Source object becomes partially moved-from; its attachment is set to null.
Any external references to the source's previous Attachment must be aware ownership moved to the new object.

functions.name: protocol::ProtocolMessage::~ProtocolMessage
functions.description: Destructor. Deletes the owned Attachment pointer if present.
requirements: No user action required. Ensure any external references to the Attachment are not used after destruction.

functions.name: protocol::ProtocolMessage::operator=
functions.description: Move assignment operator. Deletes the current owned Attachment, then takes ownership of the source's Attachment and copies size_limit. Sets the source's attachment to null.
requirements: Safe to self-assign check is present; no special caller action required beyond moving semantics.
After assignment, the source's attachment becomes null; do not use any previous external references to it.
Attachment must be safely deletable by delete when being replaced.

functions.name: protocol::ProtocolWrapper::ProtocolWrapper
functions.description: Constructs a ProtocolWrapper over the given ProtocolMessage. Sets the wrapped message and updates the message's internal wrapper pointer to this.
requirements: message may be null.
ProtocolWrapper does not take ownership of message; the caller must ensure the wrapped ProtocolMessage outlives the wrapper or is otherwise managed safely.
